sections.title: DHCP
sections.content:
DHCP automatically assigns IP, mask, gateway, and DNS to hosts. The handshake is DORA: Discover (client broadcasts), Offer (server proposes), Request (client asks for it), Acknowledge (server confirms + lease).
Components: scope (range of assignable addresses), exclusions, reservations (fixed IP by MAC), lease time, and options (gateway, DNS, NTP).
DHCP relay / IP helper — forwards DHCP broadcasts across subnets to a central server (since broadcasts don't cross routers).
Troubleshooting clue: a host with a 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address failed to reach DHCP.
exam_tips: DHCP handshake = DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge).
Use a DHCP relay / IP helper when the server is on another subnet (broadcasts don't route).
A reservation ties a specific IP to a MAC address for consistent addressing.

sections.title: DNS
sections.content:
DNS resolves names to IPs (UDP 53 for queries, TCP 53 for zone transfers).
Record types:
A (name → IPv4) · AAAA (name → IPv6) · CNAME (alias → another name) · MX (mail server) · NS (name server) · PTR (reverse: IP → name) · TXT (SPF/DKIM/verification) · SOA (zone authority) · SRV (service location).
Resolution flow: resolver checks cache → recursive query to root → TLD → authoritative server. TTL controls how long answers are cached.
Forward zone = name→IP; reverse zone = IP→name. Internal vs external (split-horizon) DNS serves different answers inside vs outside.
exam_tips: A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias, MX = mail, PTR = reverse lookup, TXT = SPF/DKIM.
DNS is UDP 53 for lookups, TCP 53 for zone transfers.
TTL sets how long a record is cached before re-querying.

sections.title: Time, IPv6 Services & Access/Management Methods
sections.content:
NTP (UDP 123) synchronizes clocks — critical for logs, certificates, and authentication (Kerberos). Stratum numbers rank clock sources (lower = closer to the reference clock).
IPv6 services: SLAAC (host self-configures from router advertisements), DHCPv6, and EUI-64 for interface IDs.
Accessing & managing devices:
In-band — manage over the production network (SSH on 22, HTTPS). Avoid Telnet (23)/HTTP — cleartext.
Out-of-band — a separate path (console port, dedicated mgmt port, or modem) that works even if the production network is down.
Jump box / bastion host — a hardened gateway you connect through to reach internal devices.
VPN — encrypted remote access (site-to-site or client/remote-access); console access for initial/last-resort config.
exam_tips: NTP (UDP 123) keeps clocks in sync — essential for logging, certs, and Kerberos auth.
Use SSH (22) not Telnet (23); HTTPS not HTTP — manage devices encrypted.
Out-of-band management (console/dedicated mgmt port) works even when the production network is down.

concept_cards.hook: The four-step DHCP lease process: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
Forwards DHCP broadcast requests to a server on another subnet, since routers don't forward broadcasts.
A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (name server), PTR (reverse), TXT (SPF/DKIM), SOA, SRV.
A DNS reverse-lookup record mapping an IP address back to a hostname (used in reverse zones).
Network Time Protocol (UDP 123) that synchronizes device clocks; stratum ranks how close a source is to the reference clock.
In-band management rides the production network (SSH/HTTPS); out-of-band uses a separate path (console/mgmt port) that works during outages.
A hardened intermediary host that administrators connect through to reach and manage internal systems securely.
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — how an IPv6 host builds its own address from a router advertisement without a DHCP server.

practice_questions.q: Put the DHCP lease steps in order.
practice_questions.explanation: DHCP follows DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

practice_questions.q: An admin connects to a switch's console port with a rollover cable to perform initial setup. This is an example of:
practice_questions.explanation: Console access is out-of-band — a separate path that works before (or when) the production network is unavailable.

practice_questions.q: Which DNS record maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
practice_questions.explanation: AAAA maps a name to an IPv6 address; A is for IPv4.

practice_questions.q: Which remote-access method creates an encrypted tunnel for a remote user over the public internet?
practice_questions.explanation: A remote-access VPN encrypts the user's traffic over the internet back to the corporate network.

practice_questions.q: DHCP clients are on a subnet without a DHCP server. What forwards their requests to the server?
practice_questions.explanation: Routers don't forward broadcasts, so a DHCP relay/IP helper forwards requests to a server on another subnet.

practice_questions.q: Which management method still works when the production network is down?
practice_questions.explanation: Out-of-band management uses a separate path (console/modem/mgmt port) independent of the production network.

practice_questions.q: A host must always receive the same IP from DHCP. What should be configured?
options: A reservation (IP tied to the MAC)
practice_questions.explanation: A DHCP reservation binds a specific IP to a device's MAC address.

practice_questions.q: A hardened host that admins connect through to reach internal devices is called a:
practice_questions.explanation: A jump box (bastion host) is a secured intermediary for administrative access to internal systems.

practice_questions.q: Which DNS record identifies the mail server for a domain?
practice_questions.explanation: The MX record specifies the mail exchanger for a domain.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol should replace Telnet for secure device management?
practice_questions.explanation: SSH encrypts management sessions; Telnet sends everything in cleartext.
